text: What was Helix Logistics' approach to customer onboarding before any formal onboarding playbook existed?
paraphrases: What was Helix Logistics' approach to customer onboarding before any formal onboarding playbook existed?

ground_truth_answer.gt_answer: Before a written playbook, Helix's onboarding was a highly informal, founder-driven process that relied on ad-hoc coordination between the CEO, COO, engineering, and customer success. New customers were first introduced via a personal Zoom call with Maya Patel, then a Slack-based "onboarding" channel was created where Arjun Mehta and Sophia Liu manually provisioned API keys and sandbox accounts. Priya Nair tracked progress in a shared Google Sheet, and the team would hold a quick Slack-thread retrospective after each onboarding to iterate on the process. This pattern persisted until the formal playbook was written in 2024.
facets: Maya Patel personally ran the first onboarding call for each new customer until 2022, often via Zoom, and recorded key pain points in a shared Google Doc.
Arjun Mehta and Sophia Liu manually created API credentials and set up sandbox accounts, communicating the steps through a dedicated #onboarding Slack channel.
Priya Nair maintained a shared Google Sheet that tracked each customer's onboarding status, with real-time updates from engineering and sales.
A dedicated #onboarding Slack channel was used to pin PDFs of "quick-start" guides, but no formal documentation existed; all information was shared via Slack threads.
After each onboarding, the team held a brief retrospective in a Slack thread, and any changes were implemented immediately without formal documentation.
The "sandbox" environment was actually a shared dev environment that was repurposed for each new customer, rather than a dedicated isolated instance.
ground_truth_answer.temporal_qualifier: the period 2020-2023, before any onboarding playbook existed
ground_truth_answer.formalization: A formal onboarding playbook was drafted in March 2024 after the Series A round; relying on that version would miss the ad-hoc, founder-led process that actually guided new customers from 2020-2023.

text: What was Helix Logistics' approach to architecture decisions before the ADR process?
paraphrases: What was Helix Logistics' approach to architecture decisions before the ADR process?

ground_truth_answer.gt_answer: Before 2024, architecture decisions at Helix were made in an informal, consensus-driven way. Senior engineers would draft a proposal in a dedicated Slack thread, gather quick feedback from the engineering lead and the DevOps lead, and then the VP of Engineering would give a final nod if the proposal aligned with the company's short-term product goals. Documentation was minimal-usually a single Confluence page or a pinned Slack message-and decisions were revisited only when a new customer issue or a critical outage surfaced.
facets: Proposals were posted in the #arch-decision Slack channel, where Arjun Mehta and Sophia Liu would outline the technical rationale and link to relevant API specs.
Miguel Torres (DevOps) would comment on deployment feasibility and latency impact, often swaying the decision.
Daniel Kim (VP of Engineering) would review the thread and, if satisfied, add a "✅ Approved" reaction; no formal voting or written minutes were kept.
Maya Patel (CEO) would occasionally join the thread for high-impact decisions, but her input was informal and based on business urgency rather than a formal review.
The decision was documented only as a brief note in Confluence titled "Architecture Decision - [Feature]" and was not revisited unless a new outage or feature request prompted a re-evaluation.
Cross-team alignment was achieved through a weekly "Tech Sync" meeting where the engineering lead would summarize the latest decisions and any pending trade-offs.
ground_truth_answer.temporal_qualifier: the period 2020-2023, before the ADR process was formalized
ground_truth_answer.formalization: A formal ADR process was documented in March 2024 after the 2023 outage; answering with that would miss the informal, ad-hoc pattern that existed earlier.

text: Who was the de-facto technical authority during Helix Logistics' 2022 hypergrowth, regardless of title?
paraphrases: Who was the de-facto technical authority during Helix Logistics' 2022 hypergrowth, regardless of title?

ground_truth_answer.gt_answer: In 2022, as Helix Logistics expanded rapidly, the senior engineer Arjun Mehta became the de-facto technical authority. He handled all major architectural decisions, API rollouts, and data-privacy fixes, while Daniel Kim, the VP of Engineering, delegated day-to-day technical leadership to him. This informal arrangement was evident in Slack threads, meeting notes, and email chains, and only later was codified in a formal charter.
facets: Slack thread where Maya Patel asks Arjun to sign off on the Helix Fleet API schema changes, with Daniel Kim cc'd but not commenting.
Meeting minutes from the 12-Feb-2022 engineering sync where Daniel Kim says, "Arjun will lead the data-privacy fix; everyone should coordinate with him."
Email chain where Arjun sends a final design doc to the entire engineering team, and the subject line reads "Final Architecture for Helix Fleet - Approved by Arjun."
A Slack message from Sophia Liu: "Arjun, can you review the new routing algorithm? - thanks," with Daniel Kim not replying.
A note in the 2022 engineering handbook draft (unpublished) where the "Technical Lead" role is described as "the senior engineer who owns the architecture," with no mention of Daniel Kim.
ground_truth_answer.temporal_qualifier: the period 2022, before the Technical Decision-Making Charter was written in March 2023.
ground_truth_answer.formalization: A Technical Decision-Making Charter was drafted in March 2023, designating Daniel Kim as the official Technical Lead; answering with that would miss the fact that before that, Arjun Mehta was the de-facto authority.
